tips.title: Keep infants sleeping on their backs on a firm surface; share a room but not a bed; and do not place any soft items in the crib or bed.
tips.cost: This costs nothing upfront. However, you’ll need to replace the mattress with a firm one, which may cost a few hundred rupees. The real challenge is resisting pressure from older relatives to deviate from this rule.
tips.inPlainWords: Always place babies on their backs to sleep on a hard, flat surface. Parents and infants should share a room, but not the same bed. Never put pillows, blankets, bed rails, stuffed animals, or special shaped pillows in the sleeping area. Inclined cribs or baby chairs are only meant for sitting — they must never be used as a sleeping surface. In the United States alone, roughly 3,500 infants die each year from sleep-related causes.
tips.benefit: Each year, nearly 3,500 infants in the U.S. lose their lives to sleep-related issues, including sudden infant death syndrome, deaths of unknown cause, and accidental suffocation in bedding. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a safe sleep environment consisting of: infants sleeping on their backs; using a solid, non-inclined sleeping surface; sharing a room without sharing a bed; and avoiding soft bedding and overheating. Additional protective measures include breastfeeding, keeping infants away from nicotine and alcohol, ensuring all vaccinations are up to date, and offering a pacifier during sleep.
tips.sources: Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I, Task Force on Sudden Infant Death Syndrome and the Committee on Fetus and Newborn (2022). Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics, 150(1), e2022057990. <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2022-057990>
tips.caveats: “Do not place any soft items in the bed” means absolutely no pillows, blankets, bed rails, stuffed toys, or shaped pillows — even nursing pillows that appear perfectly safe are prohibited. Inclined cribs and baby chairs must never be used as sleeping areas. This requirement represents the biggest departure from common practice in this section, and it often requires the strongest resistance to family pressure.

tips.title: Administer the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours after birth
tips.cost: No cost at all. The hepatitis B vaccine is part of the routine immunization program, so it is provided free of charge. It is given to newborns in the hospital on the day of birth; no extra trips are needed.
tips.inPlainWords: The first dose of hepatitis B vaccine must be given to a newborn within 24 hours after birth. Roughly 95% of infants and toddlers who contract hepatitis B go on to develop chronic hepatitis. In contrast, the vast majority of adults who get infected recover on their own without medical intervention. Hence, the earlier this vaccine is administered, the greater its protective benefit. If the mother tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, the infant also needs to receive an injection of hepatitis B immunoglobulin at the same time.
tips.benefit: The World Health Organization states: “All infants should receive the hepatitis B vaccine as early as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours.” The rationale behind this recommendation is that “about 95% of infections in infants and toddlers progress to chronic hepatitis.” Most adults who contract the virus also recover spontaneously, meaning they do not require any treatment to get better.
tips.sources: World Health Organization. Hepatitis B fact sheet. <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis-b>
tips.caveats: If the mother tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, the newborn must receive an injection of hepatitis B immunoglobulin right after birth. This fact must be clarified during prenatal checkups; do not wait until after delivery to ask about it. Details on screening requirements for mothers can be found in Section 1.

tips.title: Give every dose on India's Universal Immunisation Programme schedule — the government doses are free, and a missed dose is caught up, not restarted
tips.cost: Free in a government hospital, primary health centre, sub-centre or anganwadi session; a private paediatrician charges for each visit. You will go back several times as the child grows, so keep the immunisation card safe and photograph it.
tips.inPlainWords: India's Universal Immunisation Programme sets one national schedule. At birth: BCG, the oral polio birth dose and the hepatitis B birth dose. At 6, 10 and 14 weeks: the pentavalent vaccine (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b) and oral polio, with rotavirus and pneumococcal conjugate doses and the two fractional IPV doses fitted in over the same visits. At 9 to 12 months: measles-rubella, the first Japanese encephalitis dose in endemic districts, and a pneumococcal booster. At 16 to 24 months: the second measles-rubella dose, the second Japanese encephalitis dose where it is given, and the first DPT booster. At 5 to 6 years: the second DPT booster. At 10 and 16 years: tetanus and adult diphtheria. All of these are free in a government facility. A missed dose is caught up from where the child stopped, the series is not restarted, and a vaccine from a different manufacturer can be used to finish it.
tips.benefit: The schedule is published by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and delivered through ANMs, ASHAs and government facilities under the National Health Mission; every dose is written on the Mother and Child Protection card, which is also asked for at anganwadi and school health check-ups. India does not require a vaccination certificate for school admission the way some countries do, so that card is your only record — photograph it after each visit. Several vaccines can be given on the same day at separate sites, and a mild illness, eczema, hives, allergic rhinitis, asthma or neonatal jaundice is not a reason to postpone a dose. The real contraindications are a severe allergic reaction to an earlier dose or a known allergy to a component of the vaccine; a child on chemotherapy or other immunosuppression needs an individual assessment by a doctor before vaccination. Human papillomavirus vaccine for girls is being introduced in phases, so ask your health worker or the district immunisation officer whether it is available where you live.
tips.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Universal Immunisation Programme. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
tips.caveats: A common misconception is that children with weaker health should delay vaccination. In reality, having an “allergic constitution,” a family history of allergies, or prior food or drug allergies does not constitute a barrier to vaccination. Conditions such as atopic dermatitis (eczema), hives, allergic rhinitis, and bronchial asthma can all be managed safely provided they remain under control. Children taking antihistamines or inhaled corticosteroids may also be vaccinated. Physiological or breast milk–related neonatal jaundice poses no issue either. The only true contraindications are prior occurrence of acute severe allergic reactions to a specific vaccine or known hypersensitivity to any component of that vaccine. Children with immune deficiencies, undergoing chemotherapy or radiotherapy, or on immunosuppressive therapy require individualized assessment by a medical professional prior to vaccination. For details on the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine, refer to section 2. Non‑schedule vaccines sold at additional cost are unrelated to this free program.

tips.title: Breastfeed exclusively for the first 6 months — no water needed; introduce solids at 6 months while continuing breastfeeding
tips.cost: This costs nothing; it even saves money compared to formula. The main “cost” is time — breastfeeding takes up a lot of daily effort. The real challenge is maintaining this routine; breastfeeding must continue without interruption during the first 6 months.
tips.inPlainWords: Breastfeeding should begin within the first hour after birth. For the first 6 months, infants only need breast milk — no water or other fluids are required. At 6 months, solid foods can be introduced, while breastfeeding should be continued until age 2 or beyond. These solid foods must include iron-rich animal-based products. If breast milk is insufficient or unavailable, formula is a perfectly acceptable alternative — there is no need to feel guilty. The choice between breast milk and formula has far less impact on a child’s survival than ensuring they sleep on their back.
tips.benefit: The World Health Organization recommends initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. It also advises exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months — meaning no other foods or liquids, not even water — followed by the gradual introduction of safe, adequate solid foods while continuing breastfeeding until at least age 2. India's Infant and Young Child Feeding guidelines, issued under the National Health Mission, make the same recommendations — start breastfeeding within an hour of birth, breastfeed exclusively for six months, then add complementary foods while breastfeeding continues to age 2 — and add that the first foods must be nutrient-dense and include an animal-source food such as egg, fish, meat or dairy where the family eats it.
tips.caveats: If breast milk is insufficient or not an option, formula is a perfectly acceptable substitute — there is no need for guilt. The difference between breastfeeding and formula feeding is far smaller than the impact of ensuring safe sleeping practices. As for frequency of solid food intake: infants aged 6–8 months should consume solids 1–2 times daily, while those aged 9–12 months should have 2–3 servings per day. Alongside the meals, add a little oil or ghee so that the food is energy-dense, and include an animal-source food — egg, fish, meat or dairy — where the family eats it: iron and zinc are the nutrients most often short after six months. The food should be thick enough to stay on a spoon, not a thin broth. For infants with severe eczema or egg allergies, the question of whether to avoid peanuts is addressed in Section 12 of this chapter — the answer is: there is no need to avoid peanuts.

tips.title: Use water hotter than 70 °C to prepare formula, then let it cool before feeding; discard any leftovers.
tips.cost: No monetary cost. It only requires a few extra minutes of waiting for the milk to cool. The difficulty lies in the fact that even when a baby is crying from hunger, caregivers must still wait for the water temperature to drop before mixing the formula.
tips.inPlainWords: Formula milk is not sterile and may contain a bacterium called Cronobacter sakazakii. Once newborns are infected, reported mortality rates range from 40% to 80%. To minimize this risk, first pour hot water into the feeding bottle, then wait until the temperature drops to around 73.8 °C before adding the formula. At this point, the milk remains above 70 °C, which can reduce the amount of this bacterium to less than one ten-thousandth of its original level. After preparation, let the milk cool completely before feeding, and discard any portions that are not consumed.
tips.benefit: Formula milk is not sterile and may harbor Cronobacter sakazakii. Reported mortality rates among newborns infected with this bacterium fall between 40% and 80%. Experimental studies show that when hot water is first added to the bottle and the temperature is allowed to drop to roughly 73.8 °C prior to adding formula, the milk temperature stays above 70 °C in most cases. This process reduces the concentration of Cronobacter sakazakii by more than 5 logarithmic units, effectively bringing it down to under one ten-thousandth of its original amount.
tips.sources: Beary MA, Daly SE, Baker J, Snyder AB (2025). Assessing Hot Water Reconstitution Instructions and Labeling of Powdered Infant Formula to Ensure Cronobacter spp. Reduction. Journal of Food Protection, 88(9), 100571. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfp.2025.100571>; Sima WG, Legesse T, Girma S, et al. (2025). Emerging microbial risks: Cronobacter sakazakii in powdered infant formula for infants under six months of age in Ethiopia. BMC Microbiology, 26, 307. <https://doi.org/10.1186/s12866-025-04380-y>; World Health Organization & FAO (2007). Safe preparation, storage and handling of powdered infant formula: guidelines. <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241595414>
tips.caveats: The 70 °C threshold is specified in public health guidelines. Beary et al. explicitly state: “Public health guidelines for caregivers of high-risk infants recommend using water heated to at least 70 °C (158 °F) to prepare infant formula, in order to inactivate harmful microorganisms.” Premature infants, those with low birth weight, and babies under 2 months of age are at the highest risk of infection. Never use water that has been stored in a thermos for a full day to prepare formula, and do not leave prepared milk at room temperature for later use.

tips.title: Do not feed honey to children under 1 year old
tips.inPlainWords: Never give honey to babies under 1 year of age. This includes honey water, honey mixed into baby food, and any baked goods containing honey. Honey can contain bacteria that cause botulism. An adult’s gut microbiome is able to keep these bacteria in check, but a baby’s cannot. The same rule applies to homemade pickled foods and fermented products.
tips.benefit: Honey can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which a baby's gut cannot yet handle. Do not give honey, including as a sweetener on a pacifier or in a home remedy, to a child under 12 months. The risk is infant botulism, a rare but serious illness. After the first birthday, honey is safe for most children. This is the advice of the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics.
tips.caveats: Foods and drinks to avoid include honey water, honey mixed into baby food, and any pastries containing honey. Likewise, homemade pickled foods and fermented products should not be given to infants.

tips.title: Vitamin K injection at birth is essential
tips.cost: 0 to a few hundred rupees. This cost is usually already included in the overall hospital delivery fee, so no extra payment is required.
tips.inPlainWords: Newborns naturally have very little vitamin K stored in their bodies. Without supplementation, it can lead to vitamin K deficiency bleeding; the delayed form often manifests as bleeding inside the brain. In regions where this injection isn’t routinely given, the incidence of such bleeding is about 478 cases per 100,000 newborns. Administering the injection is estimated to reduce this rate by over 78%. For home births or births at unregulated facilities, parents should proactively ask whether it was given.
tips.benefit: Newborns possess minimal vitamin K reserves. Failure to supplement may result in vitamin K deficiency bleeding, with the delayed type frequently presenting as intracranial hemorrhage. Belgian medical guidelines recommend a single intramuscular injection of 1–2 mg of vitamin K at birth. In areas lacking systematic prevention programs, the incidence of vitamin K deficiency bleeding is 478 cases per 100,000 newborns, based on data from 42,000 infants in Tashkent. The authors estimate that such preventive measures can lower the incidence by more than 78.5%.
tips.sources: Fiesack S, Smits A, Rayyan M, et al. (2021). Nutrients, 13(11), 4109. <https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13114109>; Tursunov D, Yoshida Y, Yrysov K, et al. (2018). Nagoya Journal of Medical Science, 80(1), 11. <https://doi.org/10.18999/nagjms.80.1.11>
tips.caveats: However, for home births or births at unlicensed facilities, it’s crucial to confirm whether the injection was given. Oral administration is less effective than intramuscular injection.

tips.title: Infants under 3 months with a body temperature of 38°C should be taken straight to the hospital — no home observation needed
tips.cost: Registration and tests cost a few hundred rupees.
tips.inPlainWords: Infants under 3 months of age with a body temperature of 38°C must be taken to the hospital right away. Do not wait at home, and do not give them fever reducers first to see if symptoms improve. Even if an infant at this age has a serious bacterial infection, fever may be the only symptom they show. Therefore, the fact that a baby seems alert and in good spirits is not a valid reason to keep them at home. For infants under 8 days old, there are no relevant medical guidelines at all, so they must be seen by a doctor immediately.
tips.benefit: The American Academy of Pediatrics has issued specific guidelines for full-term infants aged 8 to 60 days who appear to be in decent health. These guidelines define fever as a body temperature of 38.0°C or higher. They further divide this age group into three subgroups — 8 to 21 days, 22 to 28 days, and 29 to 60 days — each with its own recommended course of action. Infants under 8 days old are not covered by these guidelines at all, which makes it even more imperative to seek medical care right away at this stage.
tips.sources: Pantell RH, Roberts KB, Adams WG, et al. (2021). Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old. Pediatrics, 148(2), e2021052228. <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2021-052228>
tips.caveats: Infants at this age can have serious bacterial infections that only manifest as fever. So, the fact that a baby seems alert and in good spirits is not a valid reason to keep them at home. Do not give them fever reducers first and then wait to see if symptoms improve.

tips.title: No matter how tired or angry you are, never shake a baby
tips.cost: There is no monetary cost. The real difficulty lies in resisting the urge to shake a baby when you’re exhausted or upset.
tips.inPlainWords: A baby’s head makes up a large proportion of their body size, yet their neck muscles are still very weak. Shaking them forcefully can cause bleeding inside the brain and eyes, potentially leading to death or lifelong disabilities. Gentle rocking while trying to soothe them is not dangerous; the real risk comes from uncontrolled, violent shaking. When you feel yourself losing control, place the baby back in their crib and step away for a few minutes. Letting them cry for a short while is far safer than holding them and shaking them.
tips.benefit: Because a baby’s head is proportionally large and their neck muscles are underdeveloped, violent shaking can result in intracranial and retinal hemorrhage — bleeding in both the brain and eyes. This can be fatal or leave lasting impairments. Such harm is distinct from any gentle rocking used to calm them. Medically, injuries caused by shaking or impact are termed “abusive head trauma.” This condition is the leading cause of death from head injuries among children under 2 years old. In the United States between 1999 and 2014, it accounted for nearly 2,250 deaths of children under 5.
tips.sources: Spies EL, Klevens J (2016). Fatal Abusive Head Trauma Among Children Aged <5 Years — United States, 1999–2014. MMWR 65(20):505-509. <https://doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm6520a1>; Choudhary AK et al. (2018). Consensus statement on abusive head trauma in infants and young children. Pediatric Radiology 48(8):1048-1065. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s00247-018-4149-1>
tips.caveats: When you truly feel you’re about to lose control, the safest action is to return the baby to their crib and leave the room for a few minutes. Allowing them to cry briefly is much safer than holding them and shaking them. This advice is especially vital for parents who care for their children alone and often suffer from sleep deprivation. For guidance on managing your own emotions, please refer to Section 3.

tips.title: When choosing diapers, focus on fit, how often you change them, and whether the brand has been flagged — no Indian regulator publishes a best-brand list
tips.cost: A month of disposable diapers runs from a few hundred rupees for a small baby changed often to well over a thousand for a heavy user, so the number of changes matters more than the brand. Cloth nappies cost less per month and more in washing.
tips.inPlainWords: No Indian regulator publishes a ranking of diaper brands. The bodies that exist are the Bureau of Indian Standards, which writes product standards, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, which regulates medical devices, and the consumer commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which hear complaints about a defective product or a misleading claim. A higher price is no guarantee of safety, and an imported pack is not automatically compliant. Buy a small pack first, use it for a week, and watch the skin before buying in bulk.
tips.benefit: There is no official best-brand list to check, so this guide recommends no brand. What you can verify is on the pack and on the bill: the maximum retail price and the quantity, which the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require on a packaged commodity, and the manufacturer's name and address. A claim that a nappy prevents rash, or is completely safe, is a claim the seller must be able to support; if it is false or misleading, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 gives a route to a refund and compensation. For a real safety problem — a burn, a chemical smell, a reaction across many babies — the complaint goes to the district consumer commission and, on the product standard, to the Bureau of Indian Standards.
tips.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A rash is more often caused by infrequent changing, a wet nappy left against the skin, or a poor fit than by the brand. Change as soon as the nappy is soiled, clean with plain water and pat the skin dry, and give it air time. If a rash has satellite spots, is bright red in the skin folds, or has not settled in a few days, it may be a fungal infection and needs a doctor rather than a different brand. Night-time leaks are a fit problem: try the next size up before paying more for an ultra-absorbent product.

tips.title: Consider buying big-ticket items in the order “borrow, buy used, buy new” — don’t buy them all at once
tips.cost: No extra money is needed; the amount saved is usually in the thousands of rupees. The hard part is resisting the urge to buy everything at once.
tips.inPlainWords: Strollers, cribs, blankets, and toys are used for only a short time, and there’s plenty of them on the used market with few buyers. First, try to borrow them; if that’s not possible, buy used; only then should you consider buying new — this usually saves you thousands of rupees. However, it’s not advisable to buy used car seats or mattresses, since any structural damage from prior crashes isn’t visible to the naked eye. Things like postpartum care centers and early-education classes are optional big expenses; wait at least 24 hours before deciding.
tips.benefit: Strollers, cribs, blankets, and toys are all used for only a brief period, and the used market offers far more of them than there’s demand for. The only two items you really shouldn’t try to save money on — or buy used — are car seats and mattresses. Any structural damage to a car seat after a crash simply can’t be seen by looking at it.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; see Section 1 for evidence of safety seats and Section 5 for impulsive consumption; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
tips.caveats: This book neither recommends nor discourages postpartum care centers, early-education classes, or baby swimming classes. Still, they’re all optional big expenses, so the 24-hour cooling-off period described in Section 5 applies to them.

tips.title: For children with severe eczema or egg allergy, don’t avoid peanuts — introduce them early under medical guidance, but never feed whole peanuts.
tips.cost: A jar of peanut butter costs just a few hundred rupees. Feeding it a few times a week is easy to fit into a routine. Before starting, though, a doctor’s evaluation is required.
tips.inPlainWords: In a randomized trial of 640 high‑risk infants, those who ate peanuts regularly from 4 to 11 months of age had a peanut allergy rate of only 1.9% by age 5, compared with 13.7% in the group that completely avoided peanuts. Among children already showing a weak positive skin test at enrollment, the rates were 10.6% versus 35.3%. Avoiding peanuts actually raises the risk of allergy. However, whole peanuts must never be given, as they can block the airway. A total of 530 infants had negative skin tests at entry, while 98 had weakly positive results.
tips.benefit: The LEAP trial involved 640 infants aged 4–11 months with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both. One group ate peanut products regularly while the other avoided them entirely; at 60 months, only 1.9% of the eaters had a peanut allergy versus 13.7% of avoiders (P<0.001). Among 98 children with a weak positive skin test at entry, 10.6% of eaters were allergic versus 35.3% of avoiders (P=0.004). No serious adverse events differed between groups.
tips.sources: Du Toit G, Roberts G, Sayre PH, et al. (2015). Randomized trial of peanut consumption in infants at risk for peanut allergy. New England Journal of Medicine, 372(9), 803-813. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414850>; Perkin MR et al. (2016). Randomized Trial of Introduction of Allergenic Foods in Breast-Fed Infants. New England Journal of Medicine, 374(18), 1733-1743. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1514210> (The general infant trial EAT in the remarks)
tips.caveats: Peanuts must be given only as thinned peanut butter or powdered form mixed into food — never as whole nuts. The same applies to the food itself: whole peanuts, other nuts, jelly and similar foods can be inhaled into the airway and cause choking, so for an infant they must be given only as thinned peanut butter or as a powder mixed into food. For choking first aid, see Section 13, Item 26. This guidance applies only to high‑risk children with severe eczema or egg allergy. A medical assessment is mandatory before introduction; in the LEAP trial, children with a skin‑test reaction greater than 4 mm were excluded. Another study of 1,162 breastfed infants found no significant difference in overall food allergy rates between early‑introduction and standard groups, though a subset showed a clear benefit: 5.6% versus 7.1% (P=0.32) and 2.4% versus 7.3% respectively. Evidence for typical infants is far weaker.

tips.title: Watch newborn jaundice for these signals: yellow within 24 hours of birth, unarousable or refusing feeds — go to hospital the same day; progressively deepening jaundice or pale stools — get evaluated promptly
tips.cost: Registration plus bilirubin testing, within a few hundred rupees. Phototherapy if needed is usually about two days in hospital. The hard part is making the trip even when the baby still looks okay.
tips.inPlainWords: More than four in five newborns have some jaundice; most clear on their own. Yellow before 24 hours of age, or unusually sleepy and unarousable, refusing feeds, floppy or stiff — go to hospital the same day. Jaundice that progressively deepens after 24 hours, or pale or white stools, also requires prompt evaluation; pale stools may indicate biliary atresia. Very high bilirubin can injure the brain and cause lifelong disability.
tips.benefit: The American Academy of Pediatrics 2022 guideline states that “more than 80% of newborns will have some degree of jaundice.” High bilirubin can cause acute bilirubin encephalopathy and kernicterus. The guideline calls kernicterus “permanent crippling neurological disease,” with choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, upward gaze palsy, enamel dysplasia of primary teeth, and hearing loss. “Jaundice appearing within 24 hours after birth” is listed as a risk factor for severe hyperbilirubinemia. The UK NHS parent guidance has two tiers. Tier one: call emergency services or go to emergency — jaundice plus more sleepy than usual or hard to wake, not feeding, floppy or stiff, or seizures; jaundice before 24 hours of age also counts. Tier two: see a doctor urgently — after 24 hours, jaundice not improving or worsening, dark yellow or brown urine, or pale cream-colored stools. Globally, an estimated 480,000 newborns in 2010 had Rh hemolytic disease (ABO/Rh incompatibility) or extreme hyperbilirubinemia; 24% died and 13% developed kernicterus. Among survivors of kernicterus, more than 83% had one or more lasting impairments. Pale stools may indicate biliary atresia; Kasai procedure before 60 days of age greatly improves prognosis. Since 2004 Taiwan printed stool color cards in every newborn health handbook; surgery within 60 days rose from 60% in 2004 to 74.3% in 2005. After the cards, mortality in biliary atresia fell from 26.2% to 15.9% in a Taiwan population study — before-after, not a randomized trial.
tips.sources: Kemper AR, Newman TB, Slaughter JL, et al. (2022). Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation. Pediatrics, 150(3), e2022058859. <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2022-058859>; NHS. Jaundice in babies (reviewed 2026-03-24). <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/jaundice-newborn/>; NICE (revised 2010, 2023). Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (CG98), 1.2.6, 1.7.1. <https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg98/chapter/Recommendations>; Bhutani VK, Zipursky A, Blencowe H, et al. (2013). Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and Rhesus disease of the newborn: incidence and impairment estimates for 2010 at regional and global levels. Pediatric Research, 74(Suppl 1), 86-100. <https://doi.org/10.1038/pr.2013.208>; Hsiao CH, Chang MH, Chen HL, et al. (2008). Universal screening for biliary atresia using an infant stool color card in Taiwan. Hepatology, 47(4), 1233-1240. <https://doi.org/10.1002/hep.22182>; Lee M, Chen SC, Yang HY, et al. (2016). Infant Stool Color Card Screening Helps Reduce the Hospitalization Rate and Mortality of Biliary Atresia: A 14-Year Nationwide Cohort Study in Taiwan. Medicine, 95(12), e3166. <https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000003166>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
tips.caveats: Phototherapy uses special light on the skin to change bilirubin into forms that are easier to excrete. Do not substitute sunbathing at home: the AAP says sun exposure is hard to make both safe and effective, so it is not recommended as treatment. Do not give water or glucose water to “flush” jaundice — the guideline also advises against that. Visual yellow depth does not reliably estimate bilirubin level. UK NICE says not to rely on eyes alone; if unsure, measure once. Babies born before 38 weeks, siblings who had phototherapy, or insufficient breastfeeding raise risk of severe jaundice. Follow-up in India runs through the Home Based Newborn Care programme under the National Health Mission: an ASHA or ANM visits the home on a fixed schedule, with six visits in the first 42 days, and each visit checks feeding, weight and colour. Take the baby to the nearest health centre rather than waiting for the next visit if the yellowness is deepening, the baby is feeding poorly or is hard to wake. The six-week immunisation visit is another checkpoint. If discharge orders include bilirubin recheck, go on that schedule. Full-term jaundice beyond 14 days or preterm beyond 21 days: NICE requires conjugated bilirubin testing and checking stool color. Jaundice alone does not delay vaccines (this section item 3). Newborn screening: Section 27, item 13 (heel-prick screening).

tips.title: If pregnant or breastfeeding on a vegan diet, take vitamin B12 supplements or consume fortified foods; infant complementary foods must include animal-source foods, and consult a pediatrician before imposing a strict vegan diet
tips.cost: A bottle of vitamin B12 supplements lasts several months and costs little. Adding egg, fish or meat to the family's usual infant food costs whatever that food already costs, not more. The real obstacle is a family belief that a strict vegan diet is automatically healthier for a baby — it is not, without supplementation.
tips.inPlainWords: Vitamin B12 occurs naturally almost exclusively in animal-source foods (meat, poultry, eggs, fish, and dairy). If an expectant or nursing mother eats a strict vegan diet without supplementation, her breast milk becomes profoundly deficient in B12. Breastfed infants typically manifest clinical consequences between 4 and 8 months of age: growth failure, severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and microcephaly, with prolonged deficiency causing irreversible neurological damage. Complementary infant feeding must incorporate animal-source foods daily.
tips.benefit: A Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) investigation documented severe neurologic impairment in exclusively breastfed infants of vegan mothers due to cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency. In one clinical case, an infant whose mother had adhered to a strict vegan diet for 7 years was hospitalized at 15 months old presenting with profound failure to thrive, severe megaloblastic anemia, and brain MRI showing severe global cerebral atrophy. Despite immediate high-dose intramuscular cyanocobalamin therapy producing hematologic recovery, cognitive and expressive speech delays persisted at 32 months of age. The CDC emphasized that maternal dietary deficiency is the leading cause of infantile cobalamin deficiency, typically emerging between 4 and 8 months of age. Because natural plant-derived B12 analogues are biologically inactive or poorly absorbed in humans, unfortified plant foods cannot provide reliable cobalamin. CDC guidance mandates that all vegan and vegetarian women who are pregnant or nursing obtain adequate daily B12 via reliable fortified foods or supplements. Similarly, the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) 2017 Committee on Nutrition position paper states that all infants require nutrient-dense, iron-rich complementary foods including meat or fortified foods, warning that vegan diets should be undertaken only under rigorous medical or dietetic supervision with parents explicitly warned of potential catastrophic developmental outcomes. The practical rule is the same in any cuisine: after six months, put an iron-rich food into every meal — egg, fish, chicken, meat, or a fortified cereal — because a breastfed baby's iron stores run down by then, and plain rice, dal water or fruit alone do not replace them.

MMWR, 52(4), 61-64. <https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5204a1.htm>; Fewtrell M, Bronsky J, Campoy C, et al. (2017). Complementary Feeding: A Position Paper by the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) Committee on Nutrition. Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition, 64(1), 119-132. <https://doi.org/10.1097/MPG.0000000000001454>; Melina V, Craig W, Levin S (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 116(12), 1970-1980. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.025>
tips.caveats: Controversy: The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (AND, 2016) states that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can be nutritionally adequate for all life stages, including pregnancy, lactation, infancy, and childhood. However, AND explicitly emphasizes that vegans must consume reliable sources of vitamin B12 through regular fortified foods or dietary supplements. While professional societies debate whether pure vegan feeding of infants is advisable even with supplementation, there is absolute scientific consensus across all medical bodies that maternal vegan diets require mandatory B12 supplementation. Lacto-ovo vegetarians face lower risk, but individuals consuming minimal dairy or eggs remain susceptible to subclinical depletion. Early infant B12 deficiency symptoms are non-specific (lethargy, feeding difficulties, hypotonia); CDC notes standard newborn blood counts may not detect early neurologic deficiency before structural injury occurs. If an infant displays growth stalling or motor regression, parents must proactively inform clinicians of the family's dietary pattern. Do not reject evidence-based therapies in favor of unverified alternative diets (see Chapter 16, Rule 4). Introducing complementary solids at 6 months is covered in Chapter 20, Rule 4; prenatal folic acid supplementation is covered in Chapter 27, Rule 1. Benefit magnitude is categorized as Moderate based on prevention of irreversible neurological disability. Primary beneficiaries are infants and nursing mothers.

tips.title: Do not buy wheeled infant walkers; replace them with stationary activity centers without wheels or playpens
tips.cost: Free; in fact, saves the expense of buying a baby walker. Stationary activity centers or playpens can be bought or borrowed. The only friction is declining gifts from well-meaning relatives or throwing out an already purchased walker.
tips.inPlainWords: A baby in a wheeled walker can propel themselves more than 3 feet (0.9 meters) in a single second; in most recorded injuries, a supervising adult was in the same room. Between 1990 and 2014 in the United States, roughly 230,000 emergency department visits involved infant walkers, with 90% suffering head and neck injuries, predominantly from tumbling down stairs. Walkers do not teach infants how to walk.
tips.benefit: U.S. National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) data from 1990 to 2014 recorded an estimated 230,676 emergency department visits for walker-related injuries among infants younger than 15 months. Of these, 90.6% sustained injuries to the head or neck, and 74.1% resulted from falling down stairs while seated in the walker. Hospital admissions accounted for 4.5%, with skull fractures making up 37.8% of admitted cases. Following the 2010 U.S. mandatory safety standard, annual walker injuries dropped 22.7% compared to the preceding four years, yet researchers emphasized that walkers remain a persistent and entirely preventable source of severe trauma. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) policy statement recorded 34 walker-related infant deaths in the U.S. between 1973 and 1998, noting that warning labels, public education, adult supervision, and stair gates consistently fail to prevent catastrophic accidents. Given the absence of developmental benefits, the AAP recommends a total ban on the manufacture and sale of wheeled infant walkers, recommending stationary activity centers instead. Furthermore, walkers do not accelerate motor development and may even delay it: an Irish cross-sectional study of 190 infants found walker users achieved independent walking on average 3 weeks later than non-users (61.1 weeks vs. 58.1 weeks), with greater delay correlating with heavier use. A 2002 meta-analysis found small delays in locomotor milestones ranging from 11 to 26 days across studies.

tips.caveats: Canada enacted a comprehensive ban on the sale, advertising, and importation of baby walkers on April 7, 2004, extending even to secondhand sales at garage sales or flea markets under the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act. In other jurisdictions, product safety standards regulate mechanical stability and braking at drop-offs, but cannot prevent children from propelling themselves toward stairs, pulling hot liquids from tables, or falling into pools and bathtubs. Recommended safe alternatives include stationary activity centers without wheels (swivel/bounce seats), floor playpens, and high chairs. Always verify daycare or caregiver environments are free of wheeled walkers. For nursery gear purchasing sequence, see Chapter 20, Rule 11.

tips.title: Supplement 400 IU of vitamin D daily from birth, especially for breastfed infants; full-term infants generally do not need routine calcium supplements during the first 6 months
tips.cost: Vitamin D drops are inexpensive and a bottle lasts months, at one drop a day. The real difficulty is remembering it every day until at least one year of age.
tips.inPlainWords: Breast milk contains very little vitamin D, and infants should not receive unprotected direct sunlight, making daily supplementation essential. In a trial in rural Turkey, 3.8% of unsupplemented infants developed rickets within 12 months, whereas zero infants in the supplemented group did. Follow the dosage recommended by your pediatrician. Full-term infants generally do not require supplemental calcium for the first 6 months.
tips.benefit: A 2020 Cochrane systematic review confirmed that human breast milk has low vitamin D concentrations, leaving exclusively breastfed infants vulnerable to deficiency. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and public health authorities advise keeping infants out of direct sun exposure, necessitating oral supplementation for all infants. The routine dose for a breastfed infant is 400 IU a day, which the Indian Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend, with a higher dose only under a paediatrician's direction. A healthy full-term infant does not need calcium supplementation in the first six months. A 2016 Global Consensus on Prevention and Management of Nutritional Rickets representing 11 international endocrine societies established a strong recommendation that 400 IU (10 mcg) daily prevents nutritional rickets from birth to 12 months regardless of feeding mode. In a trial conducted in northeastern rural Turkey, rickets developed in 3.8% of unsupplemented infants over 12 months compared to 0% in those receiving 400 IU daily. Globally, no radiologically confirmed cases of rickets have been reported in infants adhering to 400 IU/day.

tips.caveats: Graded B because rickets incidence figures derive from observational comparative trials rather than double-blind placebo RCTs. The 2020 Cochrane review found 400 IU daily reduced vitamin D deficiency by 43% (RR 0.57), though individual trials lacked statistical power for fracture endpoints. Formula feeding guidelines differ slightly: the AAP notes that infants consuming at least 27 to 32 ounces (approx. 800–1000 mL) per day of vitamin D-fortified formula obtain sufficient vitamin D without additional drops. Avoid excessive dosing: in a Canadian randomized trial, an arm receiving 1,600 IU daily was terminated early due to hypercalcemia risk; doses between 400 and 1,200 IU showed no linear growth differences. Non-deficient adults should not take high-dose vitamin D solely for longevity (see Chapter 6, Rule 3).

tips.title: Run cold water first then add hot water for infant baths, test water on your inner wrist or elbow before placing the child, and set water heaters below 50 °C (120 °F)
tips.cost: Free. Takes 1–2 minutes per bath to test water temperature. A floating bath thermometer is optional. The friction is maintaining the habit when tired, rushed, or when the baby is crying.
tips.inPlainWords: Hot tap water at 65 °C (150 °F) causes third-degree full-thickness burns on adult skin in just 2 seconds; infant skin is significantly thinner and burns much faster and deeper. Always run cold water into the tub first, mix in hot water thoroughly, and verify with your inner wrist or elbow before bathing. Never bathe an infant under running tap water. When Washington State required water heaters to be preset to 49 °C (120 °F), pediatric tap water burn hospitalizations dropped by more than half.
tips.benefit: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) reports that water at 150 °F (65 °C) causes full-thickness third-degree scalds in adults in 2 seconds; 140 °F (60 °C) causes scalds in 6 seconds; 130 °F (54 °C) in 30 seconds; and 120 °F (49 °C) requires prolonged exposure (5 minutes). World Health Organization and UNICEF reports emphasize that infant epidermis and dermis are markedly thinner than adults, causing deeper, more extensive burns at lower temperatures and shorter contact times. The AAP cautions parents to always test bath water with the sensitive skin of the inner wrist or elbow, aiming for comfortably warm rather than hot, and strictly warns never to bathe an infant under running tap water where sudden pressure fluctuations cause rapid temperature spikes. Washington State enacted legislation in 1983 requiring new residential water heaters to be preset at 49 °C (120 °F); by 1988, mean domestic hot water temperatures dropped from 61 °C to 50 °C, and pediatric tap scald hospitalizations plummeted from 5.5 per year to 2.4 per year, with significant reductions in burn surface area, skin grafting, and mortality. In Australia, New South Wales mandated a 50 °C maximum delivery temperature for bathroom taps, resulting in a 13% decline in burn hospitalizations among children aged 0–4 and a 30% decline in severe scalds requiring more than 10 days of hospitalization.

tips.caveats: Graded B because findings derive from legislative before-and-after studies and burn center epidemiological registries rather than controlled trials. For tankless (on-demand gas) water heaters, set the master outlet temperature directly to 48–50 °C (120 °F). For electric storage water heaters, WHO Legionella guidance recommends maintaining tank water at 60 °C (to inhibit Legionella pneumophila bacteria) while installing thermostatic mixing valves at bathroom outlets to limit delivery temperature to 50 °C. Never leave an infant unattended in the bath for any reason (over half of infant tub drownings occur in moments of inattention; see Chapter 1, Rule 12). Avoid holding an infant while carrying hot coffee or tea, which represents the most frequent scald mechanism in high-income countries. For immediate burn first aid, flush with cool tap water (see Chapter 13, Rule 14).
